newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK SEEN SIGNALLING KEY RATE STABILITY.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK SEEN SIGNALLING KEY RATE STABILITY.

text.p: Economists expect the Bank of Finland to repeat in its quarterly review on Wednesday that inflation pressures are very subdued despite strong economic growth, signalling that monetary policy will remain unchanged.
Asked by Reuters on Tuesday what they thought would emerge from the review, called Markka & Talous, economists foresaw no dramatic news. The report is due at 1400/1100 GMT.
"I expect another clear signal that inflation is no threat and that monetary policy will not be touched," said Esko Torsti, chief economist at S-E Banken in Finland.
"I think they will repeat that there is no reason to make any move on interest rates," said Interbank economist Sampsa Laine.
The Bank of Finland's main monetary policy tool, the tender rate, has been steady at 3.00 percent -- on par with the Bundesbank's repo rate -- since October 1996.
Economists also expect the central bank to repeat earlier warnings that the 1998-99 inflation outlook greatly depends on the outcome of this autumn's incomes settlement talks.
"There are no immediate signs of any overheating ... the incomes settlement is the big risk factor," said Roger Wessman, chief analyst at Evli Securities.
But unlike in 1995 -- when the Bank of Finland raised the key rate in a pre-emptive move ahead of the pay talks, economists said they did not now expect the bank to intervene.

"In the run-up to EMU and a European Central Bank (ECB), national central banks are likely to try to harmonise monetary policies and attempts to go solo will probably be avoided, if possible," said OKOBANK treasury economist Teppo Koivisto.
The ECB is scheduled to be founded in summer 1998 and the third stage of economic and monetary union to start in 1999.
Some felt that with the EMU kick-off so near and Finland almost certain to be in the first wave, it has already lost its monetary policy independence.
"Our key rates are married with German rates," said one economist, speaking on conditoin of anonymity.

Finnish financial markets are now taking their cue mainly from developments in the United States and Germany, and economists did not expect the Bank of Finland to say anything that would alter the big picture.
"It is hard to see that they would have something dramatic to say," said Risto Murto, chief economist at Selin Finance.
"I don't expect anything remarkable," said Ari Aaltonen, head of treasury at Postipankki. --Helsinki newsroom +358-9-680 50 245, e-mail news@reuters.fi
